body.p: Claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 are pending in the application.
The Examiner rejects claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada et al. (USPA 2007/0055163, hereinafter Asada) and Nitzan (USPA 2018/0325398).
The applicants respectfully traverse this rejection.

1. The combination of Asada and Nitzan fails to disclose extracting information regarding a blood volume pulse from the AC component of the output signal of the PPG sensor during application of the force applied to the skin of the user.
It is significant to note that a PPG sensor does not measure a physiological factor, such as blood pressure, per se; a PPG sensor measures reflected light.

Over time, researchers have identified particular characteristics, or parameters, of the reflected light that, under certain conditions, are correlated with a given physiological factor. Once this correlation is identified, a device may be designed to extract the particular parameter from the reflected light, and the physiologic factor is determined by mapping the value of the extracted parameter to a corresponding measure of the physiologic factor based on the determined correlation.

Of particular note, the particular parameter of the reflected light (PPG signal) that is to be extracted requires specific circuitry, or programming, to extract the parameter, and requires the creation of a specific mapping that corresponds to the determined correlation of that particular parameter to the desired physiologic factor. The particular parameter that is to be extracted may also require that certain conditions exist while the reflected light is being received.

In the applicants' invention, the AC component of the PPG signal is the particular parameter that is used to determine a user's blood pressure. In general, the AC component of the PPG signal is not necessarily correlated to the user's blood pressure. As illustrated in the applicants' FIG. 3, if the PPG signal is obtained with a relatively light pressure (e.g. less than 4N) being applied to the user's skin surface beneath the sensor,

a negative correlation exists. At 8N, the AC component of the PPG signal provides no information regardingthe user's blood pressure. The correlation improves SVG {EMBED HERE} 0.992.277 above 8N, peaks at about 17.25N, then decreases as SVG {EMBED HERE} 0.0630.273 increased pressure constricts the blood flow beneath FIG.3 the sensor.

Having determined the particular conditions (e.g. 17.25N) that provide a strong correlation (e.g. >0.8) between the AC component of the PPG signal and the user's blood pressure, the applicants' monitoring device is structured to extract this AC component from the received PPG signal when this condition is reached, and then determines the user's blood pressure by mapping the value of this AC component to a value of blood pressure based on the determined correlation under this condition.

Asada, on the other hand, uses the peak (maximum) value of the PPG signal as the particular parameter that is used to determine the user's blood pressure. Asada describes conditions that are required for establishing a strong correlation ("maximum compliance") between the maximum value of the PPG signal and the user's blood pressure.
"Maximum compliance occurs when transmural pressure (PTM), the pressure
difference across a vascular wall, is kept near zero...
"For a given pressure change, the volume change, and consequently the PPG
amplitude, will be maximum when the transmural pressure is kept near zero...
"At maximum compliance, the known external pressure applied by the cuff is

equal to the ABP. Thus, with a PPG sensor and the cuff, the ABP can be found by changing the external pressure applied to the extremity and locating the maximum PPG amplitude... The height at which the PPG signal is maximum is
the height where the artery is at maximum compliance." (Asada [0061]-[0063],
emphasis added.)
"PPG amplitude measurements are obtained by applying a peak detection
algorithm to each calibration data set" (Asada [0068], emphasis added).

Of particular note, the circuitry or programming used to extract the maximum value of the PPG signal is substantially different (and substantially simpler) than the circuitry or programming needed to extract the AC component of the PPG signal. In like manner, the mapping of the maximum value of the PPG signal to a measure of blood pressure will be substantially different, because it will be based on the correlation of the maximum value to blood pressure, and not the correlation of the AC component to blood pressure.

Additionally, the particular conditions for providing a strong correlation between the maximum value of the PPG signal and the corresponding blood pressure value will be different than the conditions for providing a strong correlation between the value of the AC component of the PPG signal and the corresponding blood pressure value. Other differences between obtaining maximum value readings and extracting AC component values from the PPG signal, including differences in signal-to-noise ratios, relative signal amplitudes, and so on, will be evident to one of skill in the art.

p.u: In this rejection, the Examiner asserts:
"Asada in view of Nitzan teach the above invention; Nitzan in the combination
"extract information regarding a blood volume pulse from the AC component

body.p: of the PPG sensor (Paragraphs 0061-0062: identifying blood pressure
information from a change in blood volume)" (Office action, page 4, lines 5-9).
The applicants respectfully disagree with this assertion.
At the cited text, Nitzan discloses:
"In some embodiments descending pressure conditions are applied over the
pressure-affected body part starting from a pressure greater than the SBP, while simultaneously conducting optical (e.g., PPG) measurements therein.

Accordingly, when the descending pressure conditions are being applied, the instantaneous absolute air pressure data is processed to determine a highest pressure value at which at least one of the pulsatile and baseline components of the optical measurement exhibits changes associated with increase of blood volume in the pressure-affected body part. The highest pressure value from the pressure values determined for the pulsatile and baseline components is then used as the initial blood pressure value of the subject for which a correction factor is computed from measurements taken from the pressure-free body part of the subject, as described hereinabove and hereinbelow, to determine the respective
average blood pressure value.
"In some embodiments ascending pressure conditions are applied over the

pressure-affected body part, starting from a pressure smaller than the systolic blood pressure, while simultaneously conducting optical (e.g., PPG) measurements therein. Accordingly, when the ascending pressure conditions are being applied, the pressure data is processed to identify a highest pressure value at which at least one of the pulsatile and baseline components of the optical measurement exhibits changes associated with increase of blood volume in the pressure-affected body part, which is then similarly used as the initial blood
pressure value of the subject." (Nitzan [0061]-[0062].)
As is clearly evident, nowhere in the text cited by the Examiner does Nitzan
disclose extracting information regarding a blood volume pulse from the AC component of the output signal of the PPG sensor, as asserted by the Examiner.

Because the Examiner has failed to identify where the combination of Asada and Nitzan discloses extracting information regarding a blood volume pulse from the AC component of the output signal of the PPG sensor, as specifically claimed in each of independent claims 1, 9, and 18, the applicants respectfully maintain that the Examiner has failed to establish a prima facie case to support the rejection of claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada and Nitzan, and respectfully maintain that this rejection should be withdrawn.
2. The combination of Asada and Nitzan does not disclose mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information to a blood pressure value when the measured force reaches a predetermined force value.
The Examiner asserts:
"[Nitzan further teaches] when the measured force reaches a predetermined

force value, map the extracted information to a blood pressure value at the measured force applied to the skin of the user via the contact surface of the PPG sensor (Paragraph 0057, Figs. 1A, 1B: gradual decreases in cuff pressure and mapping of certain points of cuff pressure to mean, systolic, and diastolic blood pressures; Examiner notes that gradual increasing/decreasing in pressure and identification of fiducial points during the gradual pressure changes reads upon a "predetermined force value," since the values of a ramp function are predetermined within a range; Examiner further notes that limiting an applied pressure or range of pressures based on another detected signal component also reads upon a "predetermined" pressure since the criteria for limiting the pressure
is predetermined)," (Office action, page 4, last paragraph).
The applicants respectfully disagree with this assertion. Of particular note,
Nitzan's FIGs. 1A and 1B refer to the conventional non-PPG techniques for measuring blood pressure.
"FIGS. 1A to 1C demonstrate available blood pressure measurement

techniques, wherein FIG. 1A demonstrates a technique for measurement of SBP and/or DBP by Korotkoff-based manual sphygmomanometer, FIG. 1 B shows technique for the measurement of SBP, DSP and MBP by oscillometry" (Nitzan
[0083], emphasis added).
As background to Nitzan's invention, Nitzan describes the conventional techniques used to measure blood pressure.
"In manual Korotkoff-based sphygmomanometry an external inflatable cuff is

utilized to apply a pressure greater than the systolic blood pressure over a limb followed by audible/acoustic detection of Korotkoff sounds by a stethoscope while the cuff pressure over the limb is gradually decreased (see, e.g., FIG. 1A)"
(Nitzan [0002]).
"Automatic oscillometry, like manual sphygmomanometry, utilizes an external
inflatable cuff and is based on the measurement of air pressure oscillations induced in the pressure cuff during cuff deflation due to the cardiac activity"
(Nitzan [0004]).

At the cited text, Nitzan describes using an oscillometer to determine an initial blood pressure as a basis for the determination of a correction factor that is used to determine the average mean blood pressure of the examined subject.
Nitzan provides FIGs. 1A and 1B to describe the physiology of blood pressure

based on conventional, non-PPG, techniques used to measure blood pressure. Nitzan's FIGs. 1A and 1B are unrelated to mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information extracted from the AC component of a PPG signal to a blood pressure value, as asserted by the Examiner.

Because the Examiner has failed to identify where the combination of Asada and Nitzan discloses mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information from the AC component of a PPG signal to a blood pressure value when the measured force reaches a predetermined force value, as specifically claimed in each of independent claims 1, 9, and 18, the applicants respectfully maintain that the Examiner has failed to establish a prima facie case to support the rejection of claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada and Nitzan, and respectfully maintain that this rejection should be withdrawn.
In view of the foregoing, the applicants respectfully request that the Examiner

withdraw the objection(s) and/or rejection(s) of record, allow all the pending claims, and find the application to be in condition for allowance.
